Grinders · the most important purchase

Why your grinder matters more than your machine.

If you spend $1,500 on a machine and $200 on a grinder, you've bought the wrong things in the wrong order. Twelve grinders reviewed, explainer below, and a list of grinders we'd actively talk you out of.

Best Espresso Grinders of 2026

Twelve grinders, ranked from the $199 Baratza Encore ESP (genuine entry-level espresso, finally) to the $2,400 Eureka Atom 75 (a near-commercial machine for the home kitchen). Tested with the same beans, the same recipes, the same water, scored on the same axes.

The top three picks haven't changed since 2024, which tells you something about how this category has plateaued. The interesting movement this year is at the bottom: there are now three genuinely good sub-$300 espresso grinders, where two years ago there was one.

Grinders we don't recommend

The "don't buy this" list.

Marketing budgets are not technical merit. These four grinders show up in algorithmic best-of lists and at big-box retailers, and they shouldn't.

  • Krups GVX242 burr grinder Will not get fine enough for real espresso. Marketed as one. It is not.
  • Cuisinart Supreme Grind DBM-8 Inconsistent grind, terrible static, plastic burrs in a metal jacket pretending to be steel.
  • Mr. Coffee Automatic Burr Mill No espresso range, period. The "fine" setting is a coarse drip.
  • OXO Brew Conical Burr A fine drip grinder. Marketed for espresso. The finest setting is still too coarse by half.
Explainer · for newcomers

Grinder buying basics, in five minutes.

If you've landed on this page from a search for "best espresso grinder" and you've never bought one before, this section is for you. Five things you need to know before you spend a dollar.

1. Espresso fineness is not just "fine drip"

Espresso grind sits at the very fine end of the spectrum — fine enough that a 9-bar pump pushing water through it takes about 25-35 seconds to produce 36g of liquid. Most home grinders marketed as "for espresso" actually top out at "fine drip" fineness, which will produce sour, fast, undermade espresso. Real espresso grinders have a wider fine-end range, and you'll often spend most of your dial in the bottom 20% of the steps.

2. Conical vs. flat burrs

Conical burrs (Niche Zero, 1Zpresso K-Max) tend to produce a wider distribution of particle sizes, which adds body and texture to the cup. Flat burrs (Lagom P64, Eureka Atom 75, DF64) produce a tighter distribution that highlights clarity and individual flavor notes. Neither is "better." For dark and medium roasts, conical is often preferred. For lighter, more nuanced roasts, flat burrs reward you with separation.

3. Single-dose vs. hopper-fed

Single-dose grinders weigh in exactly the dose you want, grind it, retain nearly zero. Hopper-fed grinders hold a small amount of pre-ground in the chute and dispense by time or weight. For home users who switch beans every week, single-dose is overwhelmingly better. For households drinking the same blend every day for months, a hopper-fed grinder is fine and often faster in workflow.

4. Retention matters more than you think

Every grinder retains some ground coffee in the chute and burrs. With high retention (5g+), the first dose of a new bean is contaminated by yesterday's grind, and you waste beans. Look for grinders that advertise sub-1g retention if you're a bean-switcher. The Niche Zero, almost any of the single-dose DF-style grinders, and hand grinders all hit this bar.

5. The 50/50 rule (updated for 2026)

The classic advice is to split your espresso budget 50/50 between machine and grinder. With the rise of capable sub-$300 grinders, this can stretch to 60/40 machine/grinder for budgets under $1,500. Above that, 50/50 is still right. The wrong move, in any budget, is a $1,500 machine and a $250 grinder — the machine is bottlenecked by the grinder, and you'd get a better cup by reversing the spend.

That's the whole field of grinder buying, compressed. Read the full guide when you're ready to pick one.
